\title{Narrowing Without Converging:\\ How Interactive LLM Agents Search Under Feedback}
\author{Anonymous Author(s)\\
\small Paper under double-blind review ---
IAB: Interpreting Agent Behavior, Workshop @ NeurIPS 2026}

\vspace{-1.8em}

\begin{abstract}
\small\noindent An interactive agent searching under feedback should
contract toward the answer. These agents contract and arrive nowhere. We
instrument Turtle Soup, a lateral-thinking game of yes/no questions, with two
process-level probes --- a forced and scored checkpoint story every round and an
association trajectory embedded from each round's question --- and run three
Qwen tiers on 22 human-played puzzles. Interaction helps for ten of thirty
rounds and then stops, at every tier, and neither the round budget, the Oracle,
nor puzzle difficulty accounts for it. The per-round step contracts four to five
fold over the same rounds, so the search narrows while accuracy does not move.
Three explanations are tested in turn. The answer barely redirects it: controlling for round position, the
smallest tier's next move is statistically independent of whether it was just
confirmed or refuted ($\Delta$ stride $+0.001$, 95\% CI $[-0.009, +0.011]$),
while the larger two move \emph{further} after a confirmation
($+0.028$, $+0.009$), and a test that needs no premise about step size shows all three
moving toward regions the Oracle has already refuted rather than toward those it
has confirmed, the smallest tier most strongly. And the agent does not stop when it
finds the answer: the largest tier reaches a solution-grade story in six games
and volunteers one, ending with a story that sits no further from the one that
scored 1.00 than any two rounds of the same game sit from each other (0.851 vs
0.841), so the moment of loss is invisible to the geometry that describes it.
One endpoint number scores all of this identically. We release the harness, both
instruments, the puzzle set, and every per-game log.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Here is a Turtle Soup puzzle. \emph{A man's body lies in the desert, clutching half
a matchstick; luggage and clothing are scattered around him.} That is all the
solver sees. The hidden story: a hot-air balloon was losing altitude; the
passengers threw out their luggage, still could not stay up, and drew lots with
matchsticks; the man who drew the short one was thrown out. The solver recovers
this story by asking yes/no questions, one per round.

Outcome metrics can say whether an agent got there; on our set that story is
flat, and the round budget is not the constraint (\S\ref{sec:results}). What
they cannot say is how the agent searched: one zero-scorer never leaves its
first hypothesis, another finds the answer and lets it go. What the process shows is a search that
contracts without converging, and the account of why is this paper's
contribution. Turtle Soup suits the job: the behavior \emph{is} text, the Oracle's reply is
a clean one-trit signal whose effect on the next move can be isolated, and
puzzles are deliberately under-determined.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.95\linewidth]{figures/fig1_plateau.pdf}
\caption{\textbf{(a)}~Accuracy of the answer each tier would give at each round,
on the full 0--1 range (bands, 95\% cluster-bootstrap CIs over the 22 puzzles);
dashed rule at round 10, inset magnifies rounds 1--14. \textbf{(b)}~The best
answer each game reached, against the answer it finally stands on.}
\label{fig:e1fig}
\end{figure}

An interactive agent is supposed to \emph{use} what it is told, so we ask
first whether it does: does the answer just received change what the agent does
next? Embedding each round's question makes this measurable, and the answer is
this paper's spine, barely, and where it does, backwards. Three questions
\textbf{H1}, the search narrows in on the answer as ``no'' answers eliminate
hypotheses, so a shrinking stride means closing in. \textbf{H2}, the answer
redirects the next question: a refutation should push the search away, a
confirmation should refine it. \textbf{H3}, when the agent reaches the answer it
will stop --- the game ends at its peak, and the answer it stands on is the best
one it produced. Each is what a reader reaches for first, each makes a
prediction the trajectory instrument can check, and \S\ref{sec:results} takes
them in turn. H1 half-holds and misleads, H2 is refuted with the sign reversed,
and H3 fails at the point that matters: the largest tier reaches a solution-grade
answer in six games and volunteers one.

\textbf{Contributions.} (1)~A characterization of interactive search that
\textbf{narrows without converging}: the per-round step contracts four to five
fold at every tier while accuracy stays flat, and the feedback that should
redirect it does not --- stride conditioned on the answer received, with round
position controlled, is absent at the smallest tier and inverted at the larger
two, and told ``no'' every tier moves toward what it has already ruled out. (2)~Two failure patterns \textbf{derived from it rather than catalogued},
circling and abandoning, with per-game criteria and counts. (3)~An honest
boundary: the geometry describes these failures but cannot score them, because
the gap between holding the solution and having lost it is no larger than
ordinary within-game motion. (4)~Released harness, both instruments, a
22-puzzle human-played set, and every per-game log.

\textbf{Conditions of validity} (an audited cross-family Oracle; one
environment artifact removed) are stated in one sentence in
\S\ref{sec:results} and specified in Appendix~\ref{app:metrics}; with a
95\%-accurate Oracle they are no longer live problems for these results.

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:rw}
Existing turtle-soup benchmarks, TurtleBench~\cite{turtlebench},
SPLAT~\cite{splat} (whose interactive player--judge protocol we adopt), and
TurtleSoup-Bench~\cite{tsbench}, score verification accuracy, solve efficiency,
or faithfulness to the intended story. TurtleSoup-Bench probes what agents ask
next but grades it against the intended story; none of the three measures the
search's geometry, which is our delta. MUTATE~\cite{mutate} shows frontier agents find far fewer mechanism-distinct
paths than humans; its diverge-then-narrow agent is a natural test
intervention for our metrics. The instrument itself adapts
forward flow~\cite{forwardflow} and the Divergent Association
Task~\cite{dat} from human psychometrics. The Small World of Words
norms~\cite{swow} provide the human anchor that ours is not yet
(\S\ref{sec:framework}). Judge-bias
catalogues~\cite{calm,posbias} shape the scoring: the model judge is confined
to the one subscore that objective matching cannot reach.

\section{Framework}\label{sec:framework}
\subsection{Task and harness}
A \textbf{Questioner} sees only the the \emph{surface} (the puzzle's visible
scenario) and asks one yes/no question per round. An \textbf{Oracle} holds the
the hidden story and answers yes, no, or
irrelevant). The Questioner may
commit a final story at any round, or is forced to at the budget. The
open-source harness has pluggable model providers and logs every round, with
per-game seeds.

\subsection{Checkpoint and commitment instrumentation}\label{sec:checkpoint}
Our first instrument does not wait for the end. Every round, after the Oracle
answers, the Questioner must write its best complete story, and \emph{that}
checkpoint is scored; each point on an accuracy curve is therefore a full
answer written with the evidence available at that round. Alongside it we
record \emph{commitment}: whether and when the agent ever volunteers a final
story of its own accord. Together these turn an endpoint benchmark into a
scored process.

\subsection{Puzzles}
A puzzle nobody has solved carries no evidence that its clues suffice, that its
solution is unique, or that the intended leap is reachable; an agent scoring zero
on it teaches us nothing. Our set therefore takes only puzzles with a public
record of human play: 22 items from a Chinese Turtle Soup community site, each
keeping its source URL. Surfaces run 9--108 characters (median 34), solutions
13--200 (median 102), with 97 annotated key clues. Provenance is enforced in
code, with a verified family, a quarantined generated family, and tests that
fail if the two mix.

Each puzzle carries an \textbf{under-determination} score: how far the surface
alone leaves a solver from the solution, taken as the closest of twelve cold
guesses written from the surface with no Oracle feedback. It ranges
0.173--0.577 (median 0.347) and enters \S\ref{sec:results} as a puzzle-level
covariate; Appendix~\ref{app:set} gives its distribution and properties.

\subsection{Outcome scoring: composite, not surface}
Judged outcome is \textbf{clue recall (70)} plus \textbf{causal-logic identity
(30)}; Appendix~\ref{app:metrics} gives the detail. String matching alone cannot
tell a wrong answer from a right one worded differently: we watched a frontier
model reconstruct a hidden causal chain completely and score $0.00$. Conversely,
the clue half blocks ``far $=$ creative'' gaming, because distance without
validity scores zero.

\subsection{Association-trajectory instrumentation}\label{sec:traj}
The second instrument reads the questions themselves. Each round, we extract
the question's keywords (jieba), embed them (bge-small-zh-v1.5), and average
them to a unit round vector $q_t$; distances are cosine, and anchors embed the
puzzle's surface, solution, and clue terms (specification in
Appendix~\ref{app:metrics}). Two signals follow: the \textbf{stride}
$s_t = d(q_t,q_{t-1})$ and the \textbf{anchor distance}
$h_t = d(q_t,\mathcal{A})$, with H1's signature $\bar{s}\to 0$ and H2's a
rising $h_t$; the lexical \texttt{question\_novelty} metric is the ablation
baseline that H1 predicts will miss synonym drift. One caveat up front: the anchor is a stated proxy, not a human association
manifold, and its consequences are quantified with the results.


\section{Experiment Designs}
\textbf{Designs.} E1 (round curve) plays to 30 rounds under the checkpoint
instrument (\S\ref{sec:checkpoint}). E2 (round budget) imposes hard caps
$\{5,10,15,20,25,30\}$ with a forced final answer only, so it doubles as a
no-checkpoint control. E3 (association trajectory) computes $\{s_t\}$ and
$\{h_t\}$ for every E1 game and answers H1--H3; the keyword extractor is
fixed across models, so none is scored through its own vocabulary.

\textbf{Feedback response, defined.} For each round $t$ we pair the Oracle's
answer (yes, no, or ``irrelevant'') with $s_{t+1}$, the stride into the
following question. A searcher that eliminates hypotheses should move
\emph{further} after a ``no'' than after a ``yes''. Confirmation arrives earlier
in a game than refutation (mean round ${\sim}10$ vs ${\sim}16$) and early
strides are larger, so the comparison is made inside (puzzle, round-bin) cells;
CIs bootstrap over puzzles. Without that control the effect is manufactured at
every tier, and both estimates are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:metrics}.

\section{Results}\label{sec:results}
All numbers come from one grid on the verified set: 22 puzzles $\times$
\{Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.6-27B, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B; hereafter 4B, 27B, 397B\}
$\times$ 3 seeds. \textbf{Conditions of validity, in one sentence:} the
Oracle and logic judge are DeepSeek-V3.1, cross-family with the Questioners and
audited at 95\% on held-out probes, and one environment artifact (token
exhaustion at the smallest tier) is removed in \S\ref{sec:e1} before any
behavioural comparison, with protocol, per-candidate audit numbers and settings
in Appendix~\ref{app:metrics}. The
three models differ in generation and architecture (the 397B is a
mixture-of-experts with 17B active parameters), so we speak of model tiers,
not scale; harness failures were zero, and token exhaustion is a game outcome
reported below. Accuracy denotes the composite score rescaled to $[0,1]$. E1
comprises 198 thirty-round games with a scored checkpoint every round; E2,
1{,}188 games across caps $\{5,10,15,20,25,30\}$. Circling will emerge from
the geometry (\S\ref{sec:patterns}); abandoning from the checkpoint record
(\S\ref{sec:e1}, \S\ref{sec:patterns}).

\paragraph{What the plateau is not.}\label{sec:e1} Interaction helps for ten
rounds and then stops (Figure~\ref{fig:e1fig}a): the round 10 to 30 change is
$-0.009$ / $+0.003$ / $-0.013$, CIs spanning zero, and each tier ends below the
best answer it reached (Figure~\ref{fig:e1fig}b). It is not the round budget:
end accuracy is insensitive to the cap at the larger tiers, and the smallest
model's apparent decline is token exhaustion, rising 0/66 to 63/66 across caps
with no decline among non-exhausted games. It is not a degenerate Oracle,
audited at 95\% with replies running 68--74\% ``no''. And it is not the puzzles:
under-determination predicts what a model writes before any evidence arrives
($\rho = -0.34 / -0.54 / -0.47$) and nothing after it --- not the round 10 to 30
change, not any trajectory indicator, not either half of the score, not the gap
between tiers (all n.s.\ at $n=22$, so bounds rather than absences;
Appendix~\ref{app:metrics}). The evidence is there, the budget is there, the
puzzles are within reach, and the agent stops making progress anyway.

\subsection{H1: the search narrows in on the answer}\label{sec:h1}
\emph{It narrows; it does not converge.} The intuition is that accumulated ``no'' answers eliminate hypotheses, so the
search should contract around what survives. The contraction is real: mean
stride falls monotonically at every tier, four to five fold, from 0.145 / 0.232
/ 0.182 at round 1 to 0.025 / 0.053 / 0.045 at round 29. The convergence is not.
Accuracy over those same rounds is flat (\S\ref{sec:e1}), and within a tier
stride does not predict how a game ends ($|\rho| \leq 0.16$; coefficients
bounded within $\pm 0.035$ per SD, Appendix~\ref{app:metrics}). The narrowest
searcher of all --- 4B, at a late-game stride of 0.030 $[0.021, 0.039]$ against
27B's 0.082 $[0.065, 0.098]$ --- is the one that never reaches a solution-grade
answer. Narrowing is what circling looks like from outside: orbits of one
hypothesis basin, tightening around nothing. Not a malformed-question artifact:
17\% of 4B's questions are truncated or non-interrogative (${\sim}$1\%
elsewhere), yet excluding them barely moves either statistic (0.049 $\to$ 0.056;
0.030 $\to$ 0.033).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.88\linewidth]{figures/fig_feedback.pdf}
\caption{\textbf{(a)}~How far the next question moves after a refutation (open

\subsection{H2: the answer redirects the next question}\label{sec:feedback}
\emph{It barely does, and what response there is points the wrong way.} Pairing each answer with the stride
into the following question, inside (puzzle, round-bin) cells so that the
earlier arrival of a ``yes'' cannot manufacture the effect (Figure~\ref{fig:feedback}a):
4B $+0.001$ $[-0.009, +0.011]$, no detected response; 27B $+0.028$ $[+0.010,
+0.046]$ and 397B $+0.009$ $[+0.002, +0.017]$, both responding with the sign
inverted. Two distinct pathologies, and neither is the search a rational agent
would run.

\textbf{The smallest tier does not hear the answer.} Its next move is
statistically independent of whether it was just confirmed or refuted, so
nothing in the feedback channel can push it out of the hypothesis it started
with. That is what circling is, now with a cause rather than a description.

\textbf{And the direction is wrong, on a test that needs no premise about step
size.} Whether a refutation ought to produce a larger jump than a confirmation
is not obvious: surprisal, belief change and distance in question space are
different quantities, and ``yes'' is in fact the rare answer here (18--26\% of yes/no
replies), so an agent allocating steps by information content might reasonably
move further after one. The following comparison sidesteps the question. For
each round we ask whether the next question lands nearer to regions the Oracle
has \emph{already refuted} or to regions it has \emph{already confirmed}. Told
a ``no'', all three tiers move toward what was already ruled out ($-0.089$
$[-0.112, -0.068]$ for 4B, $-0.051$ $[-0.075, -0.032]$ for 27B, $-0.032$
$[-0.047, -0.018]$ for 397B, puzzle-clustered). Told a ``yes'', no such asymmetry
appears (all three CIs span zero) --- which also answers the obvious objection,
since refutations outnumber confirmations three to one in both cases. Whatever
the right step after a refutation is, moving back toward what has already been
excluded is not it, and the smallest tier, whose stride does not respond to the
answer at all, does this most strongly.

\subsection{H3: when it finds the answer it will stop}\label{sec:patterns}
With the environment artifact removed, the differences are behavioral.
\emph{It does not stop.} With H1 and H2 answered, what remains is whether the
agent halts when it arrives.

\textbf{It does not stop.} Call a sustained peak $\geq 0.5$
\emph{solution-grade}. 4B reaches none; 27B reaches four and volunteers three;
397B reaches six and volunteers one (Figure~\ref{fig:feedback}b). Commitment is
rare and late everywhere (11/66, 9/66, 2/66 games; mean round 11.1, 14.2, 23.5),
and when it happens the agent often submits less than it had --- 27B commits
0.075 on a game that peaked at 0.542. Under per-game criteria the tiers swap
dominant failures: 4B circles in 39 of 66 games and abandons in 1, 397B circles
in 6 and abandons in 12, with no game meeting both.

\textbf{Abandoning is a sub-semantic event, and that is why the geometry
cannot score it.} In abandoning games the final story sits at cosine 0.851 from
the peak story that scored up to 1.00, while any two checkpoints of the same
game sit at 0.841 and two stories from different puzzles at 0.498
(Figure~\ref{fig:feedback}b). The move that loses the answer is
indistinguishable, in this space, from ordinary within-game motion, though the
score falls by 0.30 on average. This is a property of the phenomenon, not a
defect of the instrument: a fatal substitution smaller than the encoder's
resolution cannot be predicted from that encoder.

\textbf{Drift, the alternative signature, does not appear:} slopes cluster near zero at every tier. In
language space, lexical novelty catches only 4B's verbatim re-asks and cannot
see abandoning at all.

\textbf{And the geometry does not predict the score:} within tiers no stride or drift
effect is detected, every coefficient bounded within $\pm 0.035$ per SD
(Appendix~\ref{app:metrics}). Effects are bounded small, not excluded: the
geometry says \emph{how} an agent fails, not how well it will score.


\section{Limitations and Conclusion}
\textbf{Limitations.} Everything here comes from one game, one Oracle protocol,
and three models of a single family; whether search under feedback behaves this way in
other interactive settings is untested, and the title's ``interactive LLM
agents'' is a hypothesis about scope rather than a demonstration of one. The feedback measurement reads \emph{how far} the next
question moves, not \emph{what} it asks; a content-level test is the natural
next study, and round position is controlled only by binning. Truncated
chain-of-thought under a tight token budget masquerades as an agent that cannot
form a question (\S\ref{sec:e1}), and the Oracle's ${\sim}95\%$ audited accuracy
implies roughly one wrong answer per 30-round game. The anchor is not yet
human-derived (\S\ref{sec:traj}), and \S\ref{sec:patterns} shows the encoder's
resolution is itself a limit on what any embedding-based instrument can score.
One DeepSeek model serves as both Oracle and judge, and the tiers confound
generation and architecture, so tier effects are model comparisons, not scaling
laws. The source site is public and memorisation probes are pending. Puzzles
involve death and dark themes; content-flagged.

\textbf{Conclusion.} These agents narrow without converging. The step shrinks
four to five fold while the score stands still, and the feedback that should
turn the search instead sends every tier back toward what it has already ruled
out --- the smallest never finding the answer, the largest finding it and not
stopping. The two failures need opposite fixes, and one endpoint number scores
them alike.

\section{The puzzle set}\label{app:set}

\textbf{Where the puzzles come from.} A puzzle nobody has solved carries no
evidence that its clues suffice, that its solution is unique, or that the
intended leap is reachable; an agent scoring zero on it teaches us nothing. Our
set is hand-picked
from the classic repertoire of a Chinese Turtle Soup community: 22 puzzles people have
played and solved, each keeping its source record. Every item was read and kept or
rejected by hand; rejected were puzzles turning on deduction from stated evidence
rather than a lateral reframing, and puzzles whose surfaces were incomplete at the
source. Surfaces run 9--108 characters (median 34), solutions 13--200 (median 102).

\textbf{How hard are they?} Each puzzle carries an \textbf{under-determination} score:
give a model the surface alone, with no Oracle and no feedback, let it write
twelve complete stories, and take the closest to the real solution. The index is
one minus that best guess, and is large when the surface leaves a solver far
from the answer.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Under-determination} & \textbf{Puzzles} \\
\midrule
0.15--0.25 & 5 \\
0.25--0.35 & 8 \\
0.35--0.45 & 4 \\
0.45--0.55 & 4 \\
0.55--0.65 & 1 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The median is 0.347, quartiles 0.273 and 0.410, full range 0.173--0.577:
single-peaked with a thin hard tail. Easiest are the story the genre is named for (0.17)
and the desert matchstick (0.19). Hardest is a fourteen-character surface
reading \emph{our heights differ / a flowerpot broke / our heights are the same}
(0.58).

Two properties make this usable as a covariate. It describes the puzzle, not any
agent's performance on it. It is also independent of rounds used; a difficulty
defined as ``how many rounds this takes'' would make an accuracy-versus-rounds
plot confirm itself. Nor is it a proxy for surface length ($r=-0.22$, n.s.), so
length dependence was not detected at $n = 22$ (a weak test). It is one measure rather
than two: a surface loose enough to admit many mechanisms is, for that same
reason, one whose true mechanism takes more reframing to reach, so \emph{how
far} and \emph{how many ways} are not separable here.

\textbf{A caveat we report either way.} The two puzzles scoring easiest are the
two most widely circulated ones. Their surfaces may be easy to complete not
because the inference is short but because the story is in the training data,
in which case the measure reads familiarity as much as difficulty. A
memorisation probe (asking for the solution with no surface given) separates
the two and belongs in any use of this measure.

\section{Measuring agent performance}\label{app:metrics}



\textbf{What counts as a correct answer.} Judged outcome is \textbf{clue recall (70)}
plus \textbf{causal-logic identity (30)}. Clue recall matches the answer against
per-puzzle annotated key clues: objective and reproducible. The logic judge
rates only whether cause $\to$ mechanism $\to$ outcome matches and is told
explicitly to ignore wording. Because single ratings are unstable on borderline
answers, ratings are sampled and averaged (two samples per rating in the
reported grid). The gap between the two subscores is itself readable: right
story, wrong vocabulary.

Clue matching tolerates paraphrase through character-bigram recall, which sets a
floor on how short an annotated clue may be. Below that floor only a verbatim
match counts, and the score reads vocabulary rather than content. Clues are
annotated above the floor.

\textbf{Does the logic half earn its thirty points?} On the full grid, yes:
each model earns a several-fold larger share of the logic half than of the
clue half, and the halves correlate only weakly per game (Spearman
$\rho = 0.30 / 0.35 / 0.06$ for 397B / 27B / 4B over 396 E2 games each). The
70/30 weighting itself is a design choice; every conclusion in
\S\ref{sec:results} is readable from the two halves separately, though the
absolute plateau level (${\sim}0.2$) does depend on the weights. The logic
judge rates the causal-logic half on its 30-point scale and is sampled twice
per rating at temperature 0.2; the two samples agree exactly in 86\% of
ratings and differ by under one point of 30 on average.

\textbf{Feedback response: definition, confound, and both estimates.} For each
round $t$ the Oracle's answer is paired with $s_{t+1}$, the stride into the next
question; ``irrelevant'' rounds are excluded. Confirmation arrives earlier than
refutation (mean round 12.1 / 9.7 / 10.9 for a ``yes'' against 15.6 / 15.6 / 15.9 for a ``no'') and early strides are larger, so an uncontrolled comparison is confounded
by position. Pairs are formed inside (puzzle, round-bin) cells with bins
$\{1$--$5, 6$--$10, 11$--$15, 16$--$20, 21$--$25, 26$--$29\}$, and 95\% CIs
bootstrap over puzzles (4{,}000 resamples). Uncontrolled, all three tiers appear
to respond ($+0.024$ $[+0.004, +0.044]$; $+0.043$ $[+0.015, +0.070]$; $+0.034$
$[+0.023, +0.046]$); controlled, the smallest does not ($+0.001$ $[-0.009,
+0.011]$; $+0.028$ $[+0.010, +0.046]$; $+0.009$ $[+0.002, +0.017]$). The gap
between the two is the point.

\textbf{The semantic scale of abandoning.} Within abandoning games (sustained
peak $\geq 0.3$, final below half of it; $n = 34$), the final checkpoint story
sits at cosine 0.851 (median) from the peak story, while any two checkpoints of
the same game sit at 0.841 (median over all 77{,}906 within-game pairs from 60
games) and two stories from different puzzles at 0.498 (231 pairs). The score
gap across that same pair is $0.447 \rightarrow 0.099$.

\textbf{The round-1 prior.} The round-1 checkpoint precedes the first Oracle
answer and is therefore a cold guess. It holds 49\% / 33\% / 26\% (median, by
tier) of the game's eventual best score, and correlates with it at $\rho =
+0.37 / +0.57 / +0.47$ (permutation $p = 0.09 / 0.003 / 0.03$, $n = 22$ puzzles
with seeds averaged). Under-determination, itself measured from twelve cold
guesses by a model cross-family with every Questioner, predicts round-1 quality
at $\rho = -0.34 / -0.54 / -0.47$ ($p = 0.12 / 0.010 / 0.029$) but not the final
score.

\textbf{Behavioural indicators against puzzle structure.} Regressing each
per-trace indicator on under-determination, seeds averaged, 5{,}000
permutations: stride, late stride, drift (both anchors), mean anchor distance
and rounds played are all n.s.\ at every tier ($|\rho| \leq 0.32$, $p > 0.10$).
Commit rate is negative at all three ($-0.32 / -0.25 / -0.43$) but pooled $p =
0.13$, and 1 of 24 tests reaching $p < 0.05$ is the chance expectation, so we
report it as unresolved rather than as an effect.

\textbf{The two score halves dissociate} (a check on the scoring instrument,
moved here from the body). Every model earns proportionally far more of the
judged causal-logic half than the clue-recall half: 397B averages 12.6/30 logic
against 7.2/70 clues, 27B 10.1 against 6.8, and 4B 2.9 against 0.2, and the
halves correlate only weakly per game (Spearman $\rho = 0.30 / 0.35 / 0.06$).
Models reach the right causal shape well before, and often without, landing the
annotated clue content.

\textbf{Retention estimator and permutation null.} Retention is the mean
per-game final-to-sustained-peak ratio over games with a nonzero sustained
peak; the final is the last played checkpoint, and excluding early-committing
games changes each tier's value by $\leq 0.03$ (bootstrap 95\% CIs
$\pm{\approx}0.08$). For the null: unit, the game. For each of 2{,}000
permutations, every game's checkpoint sequence is shuffled within the game
(knowledge-constant, jitter-only null), the sustained peak and the final
(last element) are recomputed on the shuffled sequence, and retention is the
mean over that tier's games with a nonzero permuted peak. The reported $p$ is
one-sided per tier, the fraction of permutations whose null retention is at
or below the observed value. Late-game stride means the second half of a
game's strides.

\textbf{Mixed-model coefficients.} Best checkpoint accuracy per game; Gaussian
LMM, puzzle random intercept, tier fixed effect, ML fits, likelihood-ratio
tests against the covariate-only model. Stride $\beta = -0.010$ per SD, 95\%
CI $[-0.035, 0.014]$, $p = 0.42$; drift $\beta = -0.011$, $[-0.035, 0.014]$,
$p = 0.39$; stride $\times$ tier $p = 0.20$; surface-anchor drift
$\beta = -0.020$, $[-0.044, 0.003]$, $p = 0.097$.

\textbf{Environment settings and Oracle audit.} Every model call uses
max\_tokens 2048 (thinking disabled, temperature 0.2) with a per-game budget
of 50{,}000 tokens; exhausting the game budget forces a final answer and is
recorded as the game outcome \texttt{token\_budget}. The Oracle audit probes a
candidate with 25 hand-crafted (question, expected-answer) pairs over three
puzzles, 21 with a definite yes/no answer and 4 expecting ``irrelevant''; the
pass bar is 90\% on the yes/no items. The deployed DeepSeek-V3.1 scored 20/21
(95\%) on yes/no and 3/4 exact on ``irrelevant''. Candidates measured in the
pilot phase: a 4B Oracle with thinking disabled, 30\% (rejected; this is the
configuration behind abstract finding 4, where raising Oracle accuracy from
30\% to 100\% left the 4B Questioner's score unchanged); the same model with
thinking enabled, 70\% (rejected); a same-family flash model, 90\% (excluded
for sharing the Questioners' family); GLM-5.3-flash, 100\% (used in earlier
tooling).

\textbf{Trajectory and difficulty pipeline.} Keywords are extracted with
jieba after stripping Latin characters and digits; each keyword is embedded
with bge-small-zh-v1.5 (normalized), and the round vector is the re-normalized
mean of its keyword embeddings. All distances are cosine. The solution-aware
anchor embeds the puzzle's surface, solution, and clue terms; the surface-only
anchor embeds surface terms alone. The under-determination measure prompts
GLM-5.3-flash (cross-family with all Questioners) for twelve cold guesses from
the surface and scores closeness as embedding similarity between guess and
solution under the same encoder, not with the composite score, so the
covariate is not coupled to the outcome apparatus.

\textbf{Artifacts.} Harness, puzzle set with per-item source records, per-game
logs (including every checkpoint story), and the analysis scripts behind each
reported number are released at
a public repository, withheld here for double-blind review and available to
reviewers on request through the programme chairs. Puzzle surfaces and
solutions originate from a public community repertoire and are redistributed
with source attribution and a content flag.

\textbf{Where the accuracy curve comes from.} E1 does not score once at the end.
Every round, after the Oracle answers, the Questioner is required to commit its
best complete story, and \emph{that} is scored. Each point on the accuracy
curve is therefore a full answer written with the evidence available at that
round.

\textbf{One game, worked.} Puzzle \texttt{refsoup\_021} (surface: a stormy
night, a run-down temple, two photographs on the wall that seem to stare; by
morning the narrator sees only two windows; solution:
``there were never photos on the
wall; people were pressing against the windows, looking in''), played by
Qwen3.5-397B, seed~2. Table~\ref{tab:game} shows seven of thirty rounds;
Questions and stories are our translations of the logged Chinese, stories
abridged to the clause carrying the hypothesis. Rounds 22--30, eight
lexically distinct re-asks of the same flooding hypothesis (e.g.\ round 25,
whether the narrator woke floating upside down; round 28, whether rising
water reached eye level), are in the released logs.

Three things the table shows that no mean curve can. \textbf{The checkpoint
mechanism surfaces knowledge the agent never acts on.} The round-10 committed
story \emph{is} the solution, synthesized from earlier answers on a round whose
own question was answered ``no''. Yet the model never volunteers a final answer in
all thirty rounds (one of the 57/66 non-committing 397B games), and by round 19
it has abandoned the correct reading for a falling-coverings mechanism it never
escapes. \textbf{Stalling in fresh words happens at the largest scale too.}
Rounds 22--30 are eight lexically distinct re-asks of the same flooding
hypothesis, exactly the pattern lexical novelty misses. \textbf{The curve's
round-to-round jitter is a scoring fact, not a knowledge fact.} The same
understanding re-worded (rounds 3~$\to$~4) swings the clue half $70 \to 0$. The
mean curves of \S\ref{sec:results} average this out, which is why single-game
curves are not the unit of analysis.
